The human being is a small-scale image of the wider order of existence: its levels connect without gaps.

The author follows the older view that different bodily organs express different inner powers. He links anger with the heart, fear with a movement inward, and appetite with changes in the stomach and liver.
The soul is not built from separate powers. The powers we see in the body are different expressions of one soul, in a simpler and more unified way.
The soul is the source of the body's powers, and in this account a cause contains the perfection of what it causes in a higher, simpler way.
“It disappears with it” refers to the first sensed quality, not to the whole body.
One undivided inner power gathers the reports of the separate senses and recognizes them together.
The body of the afterlife is imaginal and spiritual, while the body of this life is material. The same soul makes each body the body of one person.
Cause and effect are connected in their being, not cut off from one another. The soul's unity reflects the source from which it receives its existence.
A person can remain the same through continual change because the soul, the stable source of identity, remains.

The author means definitions and descriptions. It is not enough to memorize a definition of the Active Intellect—for example, that it needs no matter either to exist or to act, that it has no unrealized capacity waiting to be fulfilled, and that it stands as a universal source in relation to the individual intellects that are already thinking. A person may know all these features so well that the knowledge has become a settled habit, yet still fall short.

The soul must itself become independent of the body and its powers, let go of narrow personal aims, rise above ends invented by imagination, and grow fuller in its own existence. It must join that higher intellect and endure through its endurance—or, more truly, through God's endurance. The universal intellect is God's word, power, and will. In short, take on the qualities of spiritual beings, and, in the proper sense, the qualities of God.
Perhaps Avicenna was simply not in a state to give an answer when the question was put to him. A person is not always in the same condition. As the Persian verse says:
At times I sit upon the highest roof; At times I cannot see the ground beneath my feet.

The fact that different things receive a power in different ways is one matter. But the author is right that the soul's unity is not the unity of a single item counted alongside others. It is a unity that gathers many powers into itself. We could call it a true unity reflected at a lower level.

Earlier discussions showed that all eight kinds of acting can be found in the soul. Spiritual teachers also speak of seven subtle levels within a person, beginning with nature. In a complete human being, powers that are scattered through different levels of the world come together. When no power is missing, no corresponding act need be missing either.

Plants and animals are singled out because their material parts are continually breaking down and being replaced. This is especially evident in animals. In the medical account being used here, the causes include several kinds of heat: heat linked to the elements, to the body's own constitution, to the heavens, and to bodily and inward movements. The movement of breath and blood outward or inward during anger, joy, fear, sorrow, and similar states is discussed elsewhere.

But the difficulty disappears if we attend to the unchanging aspect of each thing that points toward God. A thing's existence is what gives it stability, unity, and its own identity. It is like a fixed place for washing beside water that never stops flowing.

Perhaps the point is that animals are aware of themselves only together with what they sense or imagine. They do not know themselves in a pure way, free from such images. In that respect their awareness is no higher than that of a person who wrongly imagines the self to be located in space and time. As the verse says:
While you imagine yourself in front and behind, You are bound to the body and deprived of the soul. Above, below, before, behind belong to the body; The bright reality of the soul has no direction.

By “instruments,” the author means the animal power of judgment and the brain. By the “shadows” among which an animal shares awareness, he means the images in its inner powers of perception. It grasps an image in common with other images without clearly distinguishing one from another, rather as a person may recognize something under a general description without seeing what makes it particular.
The “shared awareness” among inner images may refer to the inner power that gathers them into one animal experience.
The source means “this fear” in particular, rather than fear as a general idea.
Fear, love, and anger have no size and cannot be divided into pieces. The commentator asks how such states could belong to an extended body.
Calling the soul an “intellect” when it has intellectual forms may name the subject by a quality it has gained.
Avicenna argues that separating an attribute from matter shows that the soul itself is free of matter.
The claim is not that the body becomes immaterial. Rather, the soul's higher and lower levels remain joined by a real connection.
A plant kind can take in more matter as it grows; the commentators explain that one form may extend across several portions of matter.
The objection is that a single plant form cannot belong to one fixed portion of matter if the matter beneath it keeps changing.
One proposed stable element is the original matter formed from the parents.

This is not simply a repetition. The question is whether an original part remains in a plant even though the senses cannot distinguish original parts from later additions. A pause in growth may also matter to Avicenna's argument.
The power above the changing natural powers is ultimately God, who sustains time.
This refers back to Avicenna's claim that one form determines one portion of matter.
A changing thing can remain one through time by continuing without a break. This is a kind of persistence through time.
Avicenna may mean that the soul knows basic first principles. The commentator says this alone is too little to explain the soul's full life after death.

Do not miss this point. Something that exists at the level of intellect does not have a firm place there until it has become a complete intellectual reality. It reaches that state by acquiring the distinguishing forms that complete its intellectual nature. Knowing the first, basic truths—whether simple ideas or judgments—is like charcoal becoming warm. Gaining further truths through reasoning is like the charcoal changing into fire. The undeveloped soul is like charcoal; a soul that has become intellect in full is like a fire that is nothing but fire. Charcoal does not become fire merely because it has grown hot. In the same way, a human soul does not become an actual intellect merely by possessing the first truths.

It may have reached its highest development in imagination while remaining only close to becoming an intellect in full. It has not yet become established in the intellectual world. Consider this carefully.
Avicenna thought celestial souls become complete by repeatedly knowing higher beings. Sadra adds that they also grow in their own being.

This means the simple knowledge of the Necessary Being. The philosophers in Aristotle’s school call God's knowledge “intellect” or “understanding” to distinguish it from the other kinds of knowing: sensation, imagination, and the animal power of judgment.

Avicenna did not, however, reach the deeper meaning of simple intellect. A reality wholly without parts contains all beings in a higher and more complete way. Its knowledge is direct presence and comes before the things known. Every existence is present through its own presence, and every nature is present through the divine names and qualities from which it necessarily follows.

Avicenna's most developed claim is that the forms arise from God's own being and depend on Him as effects, not as qualities lodged within a subject. They do not come to Him as our mental representations are said to come to the soul from the Active Intellect, with the help of things perceived in the natural world. In this older account, the senses help prepare us for knowledge: one who lacks a sense lacks the knowledge normally gained through it.
The order of causes and effects is not a sequence in time. The commentator says they are all present together in one direct act of knowledge.
If God is the source of intellectual forms, He cannot lack the perfection they express.
True simplicity means containing every kind of being without parts or any lack.

These intellectual forms are not separate beings of that kind. They remain through God's own abiding existence, not merely because He keeps them in existence. They live through His life, not merely because He gives them life. In this sense, whoever sees them sees God. They have none of the matter, movement, or other features that mark ordinary things as separate. Even the rules that govern the distinction between one thing and another fall away at this level.

Avicenna should have removed separation, independence, and division from these forms by understanding them as knowledge immediately present to God. If this is true of existences that still admit of some distinction, how much more is it true of intellectual forms that are free from matter? The answer cannot be to replace direct knowledge with the very separation that never existed and never will.

Sadra's point is that Avicenna did not always give each matter the attention it deserved. He should, in Sadra's view, have devoted more of his time to the highest knowledge and to seeking the truth. That does not mean that mastering many branches of learning is without value. Broad knowledge is one of the highest achievements and helps students who need guidance. Sadra thinks that if Avicenna had devoted most of his attention to knowledge of God, he would have avoided some serious mistakes in philosophy. But we should be careful about the examples offered. When Avicenna does not identify one permanent reality in plants and animals, this need not mean that he has forgotten what existence itself is, or that he thinks its different levels have nothing in common.

He does say that a cause and its effect are related in the kind of existence they have, and that existence is one reality. His Discussions and other writings bear this out. In The Divine Witnesses, Sadra himself explains that the Aristotle’s followers' apparent claim that existences differ concerns the essences described by those existences, not existence in its own right.
The note explains a few difficult words in Avicenna's letter: “fate,” “claws,” “curtain,” and “flash of light.”

Knowledge is one with what is known directly. Even when the object is known through a form, its essence and its existence are not wholly separated in that knowledge: what makes the knowledge of the sun different from knowledge of the moon is also what makes both instances of knowledge alike. In this sense, knowledge of the sun is knowledge shaped by the sun, and knowledge of the moon by the moon. Awareness of existence can be direct or gained through ideas. Direct awareness may be general or detailed. The first is like the holy soul's awareness of its own existence, as understood here and by Suhrawardi. The second is like the awareness of someone who has become absorbed in the reality he knows; the highest case is God's knowledge of Himself.

Knowing existence through ideas also takes two forms. One studies its different levels by examining the essences of things, their defining features, and the qualities they may or must possess. The other knows existence through general descriptions that truly apply to it: that it overcomes nonexistence, gives things their unity and identity, is the light of reality, and is the life, love, knowledge, and awareness running through all things. Thinkers differ in how fully they understand existence by these paths. Existence is, after all, the subject of the highest philosophy.
Pleasure depends on awareness, the power that perceives, and what is perceived. The more complete each is, the greater the pleasure.
The First Reality sustains the intellect. When the soul turns inward, it may discover a beauty that was already present within it.
The commentator assumes that lack of knowledge is one obstacle, then focuses on the distractions of the body.
Learning about intellectual realities prepares the soul for direct awareness of them; death removes the body's distractions.

Because the soul is linked with the body, people imagine themselves to occupy a low place in space and to belong to a particular date. Yet the soul in its own nature is free from spatial directions and times. On the view of philosophers who reject separate Platonic forms, even universal intellectual ideas have no location, time, or direction. How much more must this be true of the soul that forms them?

Intellectual universals and even particular images seem weak to us partly because we treat them as mirrors in which to look at things outside us, rather than attending to the images themselves. If the soul made them its direct objects, they would grow stronger, as they do in the life to come. Those who seek universal knowledge should use particular images to reach universal meanings.

Without these distractions, the soul could recognize that every universal has a unity that gathers many things together and a luminous presence embracing them. Its finer expressions, and the still finer expressions of those expressions, include the individual things of the worlds of image and nature. They are its lights and rays. In it there is multiplicity within unity and unity within multiplicity.
The commentator quotes a Persian verse: while the soul is tied to the body, it cannot clearly see its beloved; when the tie ends, the veil is lifted.
The soul's theoretical side reaches pure intellectual truths; its practical side reaches justice and balanced conduct.

The expression means “ox hunger.” The foreign term fān-būlī-mūs refers to great hunger: one part of the name means something large, like an ox, and another means hunger. In Persian, a very large thing may be likened to an ox.

The old medical explanation is that extreme cold affects the opening of the stomach. The stomach then loses its sense of touch and no longer notices the feeling that, in that account, black bile produces to signal hunger. Its power to draw food in is also lost, to the point that the person cannot swallow a mouthful. The stomach appears satisfied, while the other organs are desperately hungry because no nourishment reaches them. The same cold is said to spread from the stomach to the organ of taste and make that sense numb. This is a description from the medical theory of the time.

The point is not that imagining something strongly enough will make it appear as a real form in the next life. If that were so, everyone who enjoys comfort in this world and imagines fine food, elegant clothing, beautiful spouses, and similar pleasures would meet those very things there. Such an idea is unworthy of the author's careful teaching, as his explanations already make clear and will show again.

Rather, good actions, the regular practice of them, the qualities of character they establish, and the fitting images through which the religious tradition describes them lead to corresponding forms in the next life. A person may be gathered with beautiful companions and pleasures suited to those actions. The same principle applies to forms of punishment. Greed, and the objects a greedy person constantly imagines, can take the form of ants with which that person is gathered. Someone who harms other Muslims, and whose thoughts are filled with ways of causing harm, may encounter that character as snakes and scorpions.

The Qur'an says that those who wrongfully consume orphans' property are really consuming fire in their bellies. Here they consume pleasant things by unlawful means; there the same act appears as eating fire.

Something similar happens in dreams, which resemble death in one respect. Years of plenty may appear as fat cows and years of famine as thin cows. Knowledge can appear as milk, and happiness as greenery. Each action has a meaningful, necessary connection to the form in which it appears. In the next life, people will encounter these forms as realities shaped by what they did and imagined. “People are asleep; when they die, they awaken” and discover the meanings of what they saw in this dream of earthly life. — S. R.
Details about speech, hearing, and sight could be added or left out without changing the minimum knowledge required here.
Knowing God as simple, complete being and as the source of all forms is a higher level of understanding.
Direct knowledge of God's essence, including prior knowledge of all things, is also a higher attainment, not the minimum requirement.
Direct union with, or awareness of, intellectual universals is a high attainment. To know the whole order of existence can be to see God.
The commentator says Sadra is speaking about himself, and that his arguments and conclusions support his claim.

A thing's nature determines what kind of knowledge and form it can receive. Sugar is suited to sweetness, barley matter to barley's form, and a sparrow to the form of a sparrow. The commentator says this fit comes from the thing's own nature, not from an outside choice; “eternity” here does not mean a moment in time.
The note points to the second group's desire for status and leadership, and to the way desire and cunning can take control of a person.
The “signs” are especially the great signs that lead people to God. The note says that when people turn away from them, they also lose sight of themselves.
The first group's barrier is natural, like that of animals without speech; their hearts are sealed by their nature.
“Companions of the Fire” means people who stay with or belong to it, as people may be called companions of the world when they live in it and keep to it.
“From eternity” refers to the timeless order of things, not to a point in time.
Here, “formal knowledge” means knowledge about rules and how to act.

The two kinds are misery from being veiled from truth and misery from punishment. They can also be described as not knowing and as holding false beliefs. The first is a lack of knowledge, even before a person sins; the second is made worse by wrongdoing.
This points to the way actions and words take on fitting forms in the afterlife.

The first group's misery does not come from losing the highest joy, since these souls lack the desire and readiness for higher knowledge. It comes from losing the particular worldly things they have grown used to.
The note stresses that false certainty is especially damaging. It says the soul, naturally made for truth, can become filled with errors and lies.
The note says these people may already have blessings and worldly power, yet remain veiled from truth because they settle for general religious beliefs instead of seeking deeper understanding.

The note gives examples of the deeper aims of religious practices: prayer can bring the soul close to God, fasting can clear the heart, charity can teach generosity, and pilgrimage can loosen worldly ties.

Categories and rules can themselves become a barrier. For example, someone may assume that every quality must belong to something else, and so fail to see that the soul can be life and knowledge in its own right. The note calls this kind of learning a major veil.
The “first principles” are the starting points of a proof; their arrangement is its structure. The note connects this to the Qur'anic image of a just balance.
The paradise described here includes the soul's awareness of God's essence, qualities, and creative acts.

Reaching the soul's goal means more than having an external connection to it. In this account, the soul is transformed into what it seeks through its development. The Active Intellect has existence in itself and also a presence through which the soul is completed.

The Active Intellect's existence includes the lower beings that depend on it. Its connection to the soul comes later in time, but it is prior in the timeless order. The commentator compares this to an image in a mirror that grows clearer until it no longer depends on the mirror and disappears into its source; the source itself does not change.

The Active Intellect can be understood as the storehouse of the soul's knowledge by comparing knowing with forgetting. The note compares this with imagination preserving what the common sense receives, and memory preserving what inner judgment has reached.

The Qur'anic verse does not say directly that an angel is the source of knowledge. The commentator says the argument depends on the idea that created things receive from God through a fitting intermediary, and that angels serve as such intermediaries.

A universal idea is a general description that can be said of many people. The Active Intellect is more than a general description: it is a real source that contains and supports the individuals who share that nature.

To say that the soul and what it understands are united does not mean that their definitions are the same. It means that the intellectual form exists through the soul, and the soul's existence is at once life, intellect, knower, and known.

The Anqa's thousand wings and beaks stand for the unending flow of God's gifts. In each prophet, saint, sage, and fully developed person, its two wings represent theoretical and practical understanding, or knowledge and power. Its tongue speaks through them all, as God's tongue. The note quotes Persian verse: “His voice is heard through every throat, / though it comes from Abdullah's own.”
Mount Qaf is the mountain of power when the Anqa is viewed as coming from above. It is the Qaf of the heart when the bird is seen appearing within receptive hearts, through God's care.
The bird's echo is the actual knowledge of intellects and of a fully developed human being.
A physician's treatment may begin with inspiration or instruction from God.
The bird's wings represent the powers and natural qualities that give rise to the specific forms of things in the elements and the material world.
The bird's “flight” represents the Active Intellect's relation to other intellects, or their ascent and descent as they understand universal truths and connect with it.

The bird's knowledge includes the knowledge of all who know God, because they receive it through their connection to it. The people of truth share one essential set of beliefs. This is why the Imam is said to know all languages and the songs of birds.

The fire mentioned here is the fire of nature, and the water crossed is the sea of this world, sometimes called the burning sea. This concerns the Anqa. The Simurgh, ruler of the heavenly birds, is different: it represents the universal intellect, or existence flowing through all things as God's light.
